entry.title: Ch-Ch-Ch-Ch-Changes
entry.content:
Well, I would say its been a minute, but that would be an understatement. As much as I would love to keep up on this blog more regularly, I find it difficult to find the time.

Work gets busier every day. That’s not a horrible thing, but every day is different, and the best laid plans of mice and men….. well, you know.

I won’t bore you with the details, but work and life tend to really lead to a bit of burn out. Taking care of myself and my mental health has really become a priority over the last couple of years. But again…. details.

And now for the reason I am writing this. I have made a career out of linux. So much that I haven’t actively had to touch windows willingly for a very long time. Yes, there have been moments at work, as you cannot help what is used where you work (as you have to support whatever is thrown at you), but here at home I haven’t run windows (myself) in at least 20 years. Every machine I have had has run some version of linux.

My current home desktop has run Debian since I obtained it (ok, it was passed to me from my son when he bought a kick-ass machine for his gaming. I couldn’t say no, as this machine has a 12 core (24 thread) AMD Ryzen 9 procesor and 32 gb of ram. It has the most cpu and ram of any past home machine I have had.

Recently I realized that I had done so much with it over the past few years, that it was time to clean things off and re-install it to start fresh. But in doing so came the question “which distro do I use?”. Do I stick with debian? Switch to Fedora, Ubuntu, or another of the standard big-wig distros? I started thinking about it, and most of the big names each have their own quirks. Something I don’t necessarily care for about each. So I started digging in to the research.

I remember a colleague several years ago stating that they had switched to an Arch based distro and were never going back. I know, Arch….. ugh! The installation process of arch is EXTREMELY manual. It takes a LONG time to install, and you may be working on it for a couple to a few days. There is also the elitism of the community. People who run Arch (the main distro) are like people from Texas…. you’ll know within a minute or two because they will make the point to tell you (no joke).

I’m not bashing, just poking. :) Arch itself is very stable! Most things are built when installed, so that makes things far more stable. If I was going to do this, I wanted an installer so I didn’t have to dig into the trenches for an installation. I looked at Manjaro (as its popular), but the issue with that distro is that its far enough away from base Arch, that people tend to have compatibility issues with things. Then I found EndeavorOS. Its a port of Arch, but mostly for the installation. It has a nice graphic installer which makes installing it a breeze! And installing things is straight like arch using pacman (which installs from the main repo) and yay (which installs things from Arch User Repo). I won’t get into the differences between those, but its identical to Arch itslef, so super close to it.

I didn’t have to search anymore. I decided to try EndeavourOS. And believe me, I am glad I did. I have had a fantastic experience. Granted I had to figure out installing software in the beginning, and how to keep things up to date, but to be honest, my past experiences with linux and also with how to manually build and install software (Thank You Sambeaux(RIP)!! ) really make my experience quite painless.

Part of me wonders why I didn’t make this change sooner, but its ok. It happened in its own time. Here I sit staring at a laptop on the desk next to me that currently runs another distro (ubuntu or debian I believe). Its next!!

Well, that’s all for this post. Thank you for reading!

Be well!

entry.title: Booting A Chromebook From USB
entry.content:
Intro

First, a little backstory into why this post…

I have an older, low-end Chromebook that has been sitting around gathering dust. Sure, I could probably put it on Facebook Marketplace and find a good home for it…. but the specs, ugh!!

I turned it on, and logged into it to take a look around. I was thinking about re-installing it with a distribution of Linux for systems with older or lower system specs, but I didn’t realize how low they were. Dual cpu, fine. Ram only had 2gb. To be honest, that isn’t reasonable even for most of the low resource linux distributions out there. Then the storage space was only 2gb. Great for ChromeOS, as it allows you to store your files on Google drive, but not for standard linux. With those low ram specs, getting the desktop running wouldn’t be a fun endeavor.

I was going to use this as a computer for coding projects for the Arduino, but I have other laptops that can do the trick. This thing just isn’t going to cut it and will probalby just donate it to Savers or something.

Anywho, the reason for this posting was to let you know how you can boot your Chromebook from a USB drive, in order to install another operating system (like Linux). So, I am going to, at least, provide you those details.

The Nitty Gritty

Turning OFF OS Verification

Ok, so first thing you need to do is have a Chromebook and be logged into it. At the desktop, hit ESC+REFRESH+POWER. This will put you into recovery mode, which is where you want to be. Now, you need to turn off OS Verification (ChromeOS likes to always verify that you are ONLY using ChromeOS). Hit CRTL+D and then hit ENTER.

Let the machine work, even though it doesn’t look like its doing anything. It will reboot once. Once it is done, it will be at the OS Verification screen. At this point, you can either wait for 30 seconds, or hit CTRL-D to continue to the OS. You will have to go through setup again.

Setup To Boot From USB

Now you need to enable support for booting from USB. Once you are back at the desktop, you will hit CRTL+ALT+F2 (F2 will be the right arrow in the top row (->)) to bring up the console window. You will now do the following:

  1. At the prompt for login enter chronos and hit ENTER
  2. Type sudo bash and hit ENTER
  3. Type crossystem dev_boot_usb=1 dev_boot_legacy=1 and hit ENTER (You may get an error about the dev_boot_legacy portion and will instead need to use dev_boot_altfw. If so, do it again and use that instead, as instructed.
  4. Type sudo reboot

Now, the system will reboot and will come back up and put you again at the OS Verification screen. Hit CTRL+L to bring you to the legacy bios screen, where you can select your boot device. Here you will choose the usb drive (assuming you have the usb drive with your alternate OS already inserted).

Wrapping It Up

Hopefully that works for you. I wish the Chromebook I have/had contained better spects, but that’s neithere here nor there. I have other machines. If you have one with better specs, I hope this helps you reclaim the machine from ChromeOS and give it more functionality.

entry.title: Welcome, To The Geek Grimoire!
entry.content:
Welcome, to the Geek Grimoire!

I have been out of the blogging sphere for quite a while. I’ve mostly been learning, reading and working. Covid, while causing a whole lot of disruptions, also forced companies to allow working from home. While there are a number of companies requiring workers to return, some, like where I work with a global team, have found that we work just as well, if not better, at home than in the office. The WFH part also allows many of us to handle at-home things, that wouldn’t have been possible to do while away in the office. For me, at least, its been a very positive experience.

The last blog I had was on Blogger. For a while, I was blogging things I learned. Almost as a cheatsheet for myself, but also so I wouldn’t forget what I had learned. It was pretty much my brain book, as it were. I got tired of the Blogger platform as a whole, and wanted something I had more control over. Plus, I needed to get out from under paying anually for a domain name. Enter, Github Pages.

With a small learning curve, here I am. Starting a new place to dump all of my technical learnings and knowledge. I have been exposed to a plethora of new tech at the current job, and look forward to sharing it here. I will also be importing some things that I posted on my other site. (While the Blogger site is still up, I am no longer blogging there)

You won’t find any politics, religion or whatnot here. This is going to be solely for my geek stuff. I hope you like some of the things I post and find them useful in your work or hobby activities.

Without further ado, let’s get to filling this Grimoire with information.

Happy Geeking!
